name: Mandarin
facts: Official language of China, Taiwan and one of Singapore's four official languages.
Based on the Beijing dialect; written with Chinese characters shared (with different styles) across varieties.
A tonal language: the same syllable means different things depending on pitch (four tones plus neutral).
Has more native speakers than any other language in the world.

name: Cantonese
facts: Spoken mainly in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau, and in many overseas Chinatowns.
Has six to nine tones, more than Mandarin, and keeps more sounds from Middle Chinese.
Written with traditional Chinese characters, plus extra characters for colloquial speech.
The main language of Cantopop and much of Hong Kong cinema.

name: Wu (Shanghainese)
facts: Centred on Shanghai, Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu, in the lower Yangtze delta.
Shanghainese, its best-known form, is a prestige city dialect within Wu.
Keeps voiced consonants lost in Mandarin, giving it a softer sound.
Not mutually intelligible with Mandarin despite sharing written characters.

name: Min Nan (Hokkien)
facts: Spoken in Fujian province, across Taiwan (as Taiwanese Hokkien), and in Hainan dialects nearby.
Carried by emigrants to Southeast Asia, where it shaped Chinese communities in Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.
Also written with a Latin-based romanisation (Pe̍h-ōe-jī) alongside characters.
Preserves many Old Chinese pronunciations lost elsewhere.

name: Hakka
facts: Named after the Hakka people, 'guest families' who migrated south within China over centuries.
Core areas are inland Jiangxi and Guangdong, with communities across Taiwan and overseas.
Not centred on one province the way other Chinese varieties are, reflecting a history of migration.
Closer in some features to older northern Chinese than to its Cantonese and Hokkien neighbours.

name: Japanese
facts: The national language of Japan, spoken almost nowhere else as a native language.
Written with a mix of Chinese-derived kanji and two native syllabaries, hiragana and katakana.
Has distinct levels of politeness and formality built into its grammar.
Its origins are debated; it is not clearly related to Chinese or Korean.

name: Korean
facts: Spoken on the Korean peninsula, divided between North and South Korea.
Written with Hangul, a featural alphabet designed in the 15th century under King Sejong.
A language isolate by most classifications, with no firmly established relatives.
Uses an elaborate system of speech levels marking respect toward the listener.

name: Vietnamese
facts: The national language of Vietnam, also spoken by large diaspora communities abroad.
A tonal language with six tones, written in a Latin alphabet with added diacritics (Quốc Ngữ).
Heavily influenced by Chinese vocabulary after a millennium of Chinese rule, despite being unrelated structurally.
Replaced Chinese characters and a Chinese-derived script (chữ Nôm) only in the 20th century.

name: Thai
facts: The national language of Thailand, written in its own script derived from Khmer and ultimately Indian scripts.
A tonal language with five tones that change a word's meaning.
Closely related to Lao, with speakers often able to understand each other.
Has distinct pronoun and vocabulary choices depending on the speaker's social status and gender.

name: Lao
facts: The national language of Laos, closely related to and largely mutually intelligible with Thai.
Written in the Lao script, a Brahmic script related to Thai's.
More native speakers of Lao-related Isan dialects live across the border in northeast Thailand than in Laos itself.
A tonal language, with the number of tones varying by dialect.

name: Khmer
endonym: ភាសាខ្មែរ (Phiəsaa Khmae)
facts: The national language of Cambodia, carved on the temples of Angkor over a thousand years ago.
Unlike most neighbouring languages, Khmer is not tonal.
Written in the Khmer script, the longest alphabet in the world with over 70 letters.
Has borrowed extensively from Sanskrit and Pali through Buddhist and Hindu influence.

name: Burmese
endonym: မြန်မာဘာသာ (Myanma bhasa)

thanks.text: ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်

facts: The official language of Myanmar, spoken by the Bamar majority and used as a lingua franca by other groups.
A tonal language written in a rounded script shared with Mon and Shan.
Related to Tibetan, far up the Sino-Tibetan family tree, though the two look nothing alike today.
Shan, Kachin, Karen and other minority languages remain widely spoken in Myanmar's border states.

name: Malay
facts: Official language of Malaysia and Brunei, and one of Singapore's four official languages.
Standard Indonesian is its own standardised form of the same Malay language family.
Was long the trade lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia, written historically in Jawi (Arabic-based) script.
Shares most grammar and core vocabulary with Indonesian, though vocabulary and spelling diverge in places.

name: Indonesian
facts: The national language of Indonesia, a standardised form of Malay adopted at independence.
Serves as a unifying lingua franca across an archipelago with over 700 local languages.
Written in the Latin alphabet with straightforward, mostly phonetic spelling.
Most Indonesians grow up speaking a regional language at home and learn Indonesian at school.

name: Javanese
facts: Spoken across central and eastern Java, home to more native speakers than any other language without national official status.
Has an elaborate system of speech levels used depending on the listener's age and status.
Traditionally written in its own Javanese script, though Latin script dominates today.
Not the national language of Indonesia, which is a standardised Malay instead.

name: Sundanese
facts: Spoken in West Java and Banten, in the highlands around Bandung.
The second most-spoken home language of Indonesia after Javanese.
Once written in its own Sundanese script, now mostly in Latin letters.
Distinct from Javanese despite being a close geographic and linguistic neighbour.

name: Tagalog (Filipino)
facts: Spoken natively in Manila and the surrounding provinces of southern and central Luzon.
Standardised as Filipino, the national language of the Philippines, and taught nationwide.
Absorbed heavy Spanish and, more recently, English vocabulary.
The Philippines has over 180 languages; Tagalog speakers are a large plurality, not a majority.

name: Cebuano
facts: Spoken across Cebu, Bohol, Negros Oriental, Leyte and much of northern and eastern Mindanao.
By some counts has more native speakers than Tagalog, though it has no official national status.
Also called Bisaya or Binisaya by its own speakers, one of several Visayan languages.
Closely related to, but distinct from, Hiligaynon and Waray, spoken in nearby islands.

name: Hindi
facts: One of India's two national-level official languages, alongside English.
Centred on the 'Hindi belt' of north India: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and neighbours.
Written in Devanagari, shared with Sanskrit and Marathi.
Shares a largely common spoken grammar with Urdu, though the two use different scripts and formal vocabulary.

name: Urdu
facts: The national language of Pakistan, though most Pakistanis speak Punjabi, Pashto, Sindhi or another language at home.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script, unlike its close relative Hindi which uses Devanagari.
Spoken daily in the home by a sizeable minority, especially in Pakistani cities like Karachi, and parts of north India.
Grammatically very close to Hindi; the two are often considered one spoken language with two literary traditions.

name: Bengali
facts: The national language of Bangladesh and official language of the Indian state of West Bengal.
One of the most-spoken languages in the world, with speakers concentrated in the Bengal delta.
Its own 1952 language movement in East Pakistan helped lead to the creation of Bangladesh.
Uses the Bengali script, also used to write Assamese.

name: Punjabi
facts: Split by the 1947 partition of Punjab between India and Pakistan.
In India it is written in the Gurmukhi script, associated with Sikhism; in Pakistan, in a Perso-Arabic script, Shahmukhi.
Has more native speakers in Pakistan than in India, though it holds no national official status there.
A tonal language, unusual among Indo-Aryan languages.

name: Marathi
facts: Official language of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai.
One of the oldest Indo-Aryan literary languages, with records going back over a thousand years.
Written in Devanagari, the same script used for Hindi and Sanskrit.
Has a rich tradition of saint-poetry and, more recently, Marathi cinema and theatre.

name: Gujarati
facts: Official language of Gujarat state in western India; Mahatma Gandhi's native language.
Its script dropped the horizontal headline found in Devanagari.
Carried worldwide by a large Gujarati trading and emigrant diaspora, especially in East Africa and the UK.
Closely related to Hindi and Rajasthani, within the Indo-Aryan family.

name: Kannada
facts: Official language of Karnataka state, home to Bangalore.
A Dravidian language, unrelated to the Indo-Aryan languages of north India.
Has one of the oldest continuous literary traditions among Dravidian languages, dating back over 1,500 years.
Written in its own rounded script, related to Telugu's.

name: Malayalam
facts: Official language of Kerala state in southwestern India.
Split off from Tamil roughly a thousand years ago and developed its own script.
Its script contains among the largest number of letters of any Indian script.
Kerala has one of India's largest diaspora communities in the Gulf states, carrying Malayalam abroad.

name: Telugu
facts: Official language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, spoken around Hyderabad.
Has the most native speakers of any Dravidian language.
Nicknamed the 'Italian of the East' by colonial-era observers for its vowel-rich, melodic sound.
Written in its own rounded Telugu script, closely related to Kannada's.

name: Tamil
facts: Official language of Tamil Nadu state in India and of Sri Lanka and Singapore.
One of the longest continuously used languages in the world, with literature going back over two thousand years.
Written in its own looping Tamil script.
Resisted Sanskrit influence more than most other Indian languages, keeping a largely native vocabulary.

name: Odia
facts: Official language of Odisha state on India's east coast.
Written in its own rounded script, shaped historically by writing on palm leaves.
One of India's languages recognised as 'classical' for the age of its literature.
Closely related to Bengali and Assamese, its eastern Indo-Aryan neighbours.

name: Assamese
facts: Official language of Assam state in India's northeast.
The easternmost of the Indo-Aryan languages, bordering Tibeto-Burman and Tai languages.
Shares its script, with minor letter differences, with Bengali.
Has its own distinct sound, including a voiceless velar fricative absent from most Indian languages.

name: Maithili
facts: Spoken in the Mithila region of northern Bihar, India, and the adjoining Madhesh plains of Nepal.
Recognised as one of Nepal's official provincial languages and listed among India's scheduled languages.
Long counted by India's census as a dialect of Hindi before gaining separate recognition in 2003.
Has its own classical literary tradition, including the poetry of Vidyapati.

name: Bhojpuri
facts: Spoken across western Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, often grouped with Hindi in censuses.
Carried by 19th-century indentured labourers to Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, Guyana and Suriname, where it is still spoken.
Famous for its own film industry, 'Bhojpuri cinema', based in Patna and Mumbai.
Closely related to, but distinct from, neighbouring Maithili and Awadhi.

name: Nepali
facts: The official and most widely used language of Nepal, home to over 120 languages.
Also an official state language in the Indian state of Sikkim and widely spoken in Darjeeling.
Written in Devanagari, like Hindi and Sanskrit.
Spread historically with the Gorkha kingdom's expansion across the Himalayas.

name: Sinhala
facts: The majority language of Sri Lanka, spoken mostly outside the Tamil-majority north and east.
An Indo-Aryan language isolated far south among Dravidian neighbours, reaching the island around the 5th century BCE.
Written in its own rounded Sinhala script, related to other Brahmic scripts.
Co-official with Tamil at the national level since Sri Lanka's constitution recognised both.

name: Dhivehi
facts: The national language of the Maldives, the only Indo-Aryan language spoken entirely south of India.
Written right-to-left in Thaana, a unique script developed in the 16th-18th centuries.
Closely related to Sinhala of Sri Lanka, its nearest linguistic relative.
Has absorbed Arabic vocabulary through centuries of Islamic influence.

name: Dzongkha
facts: The national language of Bhutan, named after the dzong fortress-monasteries where officials once governed.
Written in the Tibetan script, shared with Tibetan itself.
A Tibetic language, related to Tibetan but not mutually intelligible with it.
Only became Bhutan's standardised national language in the 1970s, alongside many other local languages.

name: Sindhi
facts: Spoken mainly in Sindh province, Pakistan, home to the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script in Pakistan, and in Devanagari by Sindhi Hindus in India.
An official provincial language of Sindh, though not a national-level official language of Pakistan.
Has one of the largest consonant inventories of any Indo-Aryan language, including implosive sounds.

name: Balochi
facts: Spoken across Balochistan, split between Pakistan, Iran and a corner of Afghanistan.
A Northwestern Iranian language, related to Kurdish and Persian but not mutually intelligible with either.
Has no national official status in any of the three countries where it is spoken.
Traditionally has a strong oral epic and ballad tradition among Baloch tribes.

name: Pashto
facts: Co-official language of Afghanistan alongside Dari, dominant in the south and east.
Also widely spoken across the border in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and former tribal areas.
The traditional language of the Pashtun people and of Pashtunwali tribal custom.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script with extra letters for sounds not found in Persian.

name: Persian
facts: Official language of Iran (as Farsi), Afghanistan (as Dari) and Tajikistan (as Tajik, in Cyrillic).
A classical language of poetry, home to Rumi, Hafez and Omar Khayyam.
Written in a Perso-Arabic script in Iran and Afghanistan, but in Cyrillic in Tajikistan.
Served for centuries as the literary and administrative language across much of Central and South Asia.

name: Tajik
facts: The national language of Tajikistan, a form of Persian written in the Cyrillic alphabet.
Mutually intelligible with Dari and Farsi despite the different scripts, a legacy of Soviet-era script reform.
Also spoken by a Tajik minority in northern Afghanistan.
Retains some older Persian vocabulary that has shifted meaning in modern Iranian Farsi.

name: Kurdish
facts: Spoken across a region straddling Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria known as Kurdistan.
Co-official, alongside Arabic, at the national level in Iraq, and official within the Kurdistan Region.
Written in a Latin-based alphabet in Turkey and Syria, and an Arabic-based one in Iraq and Iran.
Not a single uniform language but a group of related varieties, chiefly Kurmanji and Sorani.

name: Turkish
facts: The national language of Turkey and one of the official languages of Cyprus.
Switched from a Perso-Arabic script to the Latin alphabet in a 1928 reform under Atatürk.
An agglutinative language, building long words by stacking suffixes onto a root.
Part of the Turkic family, related to Azerbaijani, Uzbek and other Central Asian languages.

name: Azerbaijani
facts: The national language of Azerbaijan, written in the Latin alphabet since the 1990s.
More native speakers live in Iran's Azerbaijan provinces than in Azerbaijan itself.
Closely related to Turkish, with a good degree of mutual intelligibility.
Was written in Cyrillic during the Soviet period, before switching to Latin script.

name: Uzbek
facts: The national language of Uzbekistan, the most populous country in Central Asia.
Officially switching from Cyrillic to a Latin alphabet, a transition still in progress.
Has a significant Uzbek-speaking minority in northern Afghanistan.
A Turkic language with heavy historical borrowing from Persian, reflecting Silk Road contact.

name: Kazakh
facts: The national language of Kazakhstan, the largest country in Central Asia by area.
Still mainly written in Cyrillic, with a long-planned transition to Latin script underway.
A Kipchak Turkic language, closely related to Kyrgyz.
Historically tied to nomadic herding culture on the Central Asian steppe.

name: Kyrgyz
facts: The national language of Kyrgyzstan, a mountainous Central Asian country.
Written in the Cyrillic alphabet, introduced during the Soviet period.
Closely related to Kazakh, with speakers often able to understand each other.
Home to the Manas, one of the world's longest epic poems, traditionally recited from memory.

name: Turkmen
facts: The national language of Turkmenistan, one of the most sparsely populated countries in Central Asia.
An Oghuz Turkic language, closely related to Turkish and Azerbaijani.
Switched from Cyrillic to a Latin-based alphabet after independence in 1991.
Also spoken by a Turkmen minority in northern Afghanistan and northeastern Iran.

name: Uyghur
facts: Spoken by the Uyghur people, concentrated in the Xinjiang region of northwest China.
A Turkic language, unrelated to Mandarin Chinese, written in a modified Perso-Arabic script.
Not an official language of China at the national level, though it has regional use in Xinjiang.
Historically a language of the Silk Road oases of the Tarim Basin.

name: Tatar
facts: The largest Turkic language of Russia, centred on Tatarstan on the Volga River.
Co-official with Russian within the Republic of Tatarstan, though not at the national level.
Written in Cyrillic since the Soviet period, after earlier use of Arabic and briefly Latin script.
Also widely spoken by Bashkirs and others in neighbouring Bashkortostan.

name: Mongolian
facts: The national language of Mongolia, written there in the Cyrillic alphabet.
Also spoken in China's Inner Mongolia, where the traditional vertical Mongolian script is still used.
A Mongolic language, a small family distinct from the neighbouring Turkic and Sino-Tibetan languages.
Historically the language of the Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan.

name: Tibetan

bye.say: kah-lay PAY (to someone leaving; ga le zhu to someone staying)

facts: Spoken across the Tibetan Plateau, chiefly in China's Xizang (Tibet) Autonomous Region.
Written in the Tibetan script, adapted from an Indian Brahmic script in the 7th century.
Tonal in some dialects, including Standard Tibetan (Lhasa dialect), unlike most other Tibetic varieties.
The liturgical language of Tibetan Buddhism, used well beyond the Tibetan Plateau itself.

name: Georgian
facts: The national language of Georgia, in the South Caucasus.
Written in its own unique Georgian script, with no close relatives outside the Kartvelian family.
Not related to Indo-European, Turkic or Semitic languages despite its location at their crossroads.
Has a famously complex verb system with many prefixes and suffixes marking person and case.

name: Armenian
facts: The national language of Armenia, forming its own branch of the Indo-European family.
Written in a unique 36-letter alphabet created around 405 CE by Mesrop Mashtots.
Split historically into Eastern Armenian (spoken in Armenia) and Western Armenian (spoken by the diaspora).
Armenia was among the first states to adopt Christianity, shaping centuries of Armenian literature.

name: Hebrew
facts: The official language of Israel, written right-to-left in the Hebrew alphabet.
Revived as an everyday spoken language in the late 19th and 20th centuries after surviving mainly as a liturgical language.
A Semitic language, related to Arabic and Aramaic.
Also the language of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), composed over roughly a thousand years.
